subject: method_CPM_vs_DSC
magnitude: CPM (or polarised microscopy) minus DSC = +1.9 to +10.45 C, mean +6.1 C, median +4.4 C, n=5 same-source oils
conditions: Same paper, same oil: Kumkol +1.9 and Uzen +4.1 (Sigitov 2014, PLM range midpoint vs DSC 1 C/min), DJ crude +4.4 (CIESC 2020), Dabei A +9.85 and Dabei B +10.45 (Cao 2022 condensates, 1 atm). Derived from master_v9.csv
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv (this study)
notes: Cross-source CPM vs DSC pairs (Garden Banks +8.9, Penara +26 to +31) are larger but mix samples and labs, so not used. The two condensates with low wax (Dabei) show the biggest gap, consistent with DSC needing more solid to register.

subject: method_DSC_vs_FTIR
magnitude: DSC minus FTIR = mean +0.45 C, SD 2.25 C, range -4.0 to +5.0 C, mean absolute 1.55 C, n=10 oils
conditions: 10 Brazilian crudes (Bouzas 2011, five paraffinic CP and five naphthenic CN), both methods in same study
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv, rows R298 to R317 (Bouzas 2011)
notes: DSC and FTIR are statistically indistinguishable on these oils; use zero mean offset with about 2 C scatter.

subject: method_CPM_vs_viscometry
magnitude: CPM minus viscometry (history erased) = mean -2.2 C, median +1.1 C, SD 7.6 C, range -18.2 to +4.7 C, n=14 Alaska North Slope dead oils
conditions: Anyanwu 2007 UAF MS thesis, ANS stock tank oils, CPM vs break in viscosity-temperature curve after heating to erase thermal history
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv (Anyanwu 2007 rows R246 to R279)
notes: Median near zero; three oils (s03, s10, s14) give viscometric WAT 15 to 18 C above CPM, which looks like a different physical event or a reading problem. For a generator, viscometry about equal to CPM with heavy tails.

subject: thermal_history
magnitude: Viscometric WAT with previous thermal history kept is 3.6 to 8.8 C (mean 5.6 C) lower than with history erased; CPM minus history-kept viscometry = +5.4 to +13.5 C (mean 9.2 C)
conditions: 3 ANS dead oils (s04, s05, s06), Anyanwu 2007
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv (Anyanwu 2007)
where: rows R263 to R265 vs R280 to R282
notes: Not heating the sample to erase crystal memory lowers the apparent WAT by several degrees.

subject: WDT
magnitude: WDT minus WAT = mean +9.2 C, median +8.2 C, SD 5.6 C, range -7.8 to +22.0 C, n=39 rows
conditions: All master_v9 rows with both WAT and WDT: ANS CPM (14), Kok 2018 Turkish DSC (8), Nordin 2014 rheometer (5), KG-D6 D8420 (5), Chulalongkorn DSC (3), others
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: One negative value (Kok 2018 oil 8, WDT 30.0 below WAT 37.8) is probably a transcription or source error; excluding it, minimum is +2.2 C.

subject: WDT
magnitude: WDT minus WAT by CPM = mean +8.5 C, median +8.0 C, range +4.3 to +13.3 C, n=14
conditions: ANS dead oils, CPM heating vs cooling, Anyanwu 2007
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv (Anyanwu 2007)

subject: WDT
magnitude: WDT minus WAT by ASTM D8420/IP 389A = +3.6 to +7.6 C, mean about 6 C, n=7 samples
conditions: KG-D6 condensate (5 assays) and MJ-N4A crude, Bureau Veritas / Intertek, Reliance tenders
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv (Reliance assays)

subject: WDT
magnitude: WDT minus WAT by DSC at 2 C/min = +2.2 to +14.9 C (7 oils), median +12.1 C
conditions: 8 Turkish crudes, DSC cooling 2 C/min 60 to -20 C, Kok et al. 2018 J Pet Sci Eng 168:542
citation: Kok, Varfolomeev and Nurgaliev (2018). J Pet Sci Eng 168:542-545, via master_v9.csv
notes: Oil 8 gives WDT below WAT, likely error, excluded from range.

subject: WDT
magnitude: WDT minus WAT by rheometer flow curve = +2.3 to +10.6 C, mean 5.9 C, n=5
conditions: Malaysian light and heavy crudes, Discovery hybrid rheometer, Nordin 2014 UTP report
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv (Nordin 2014)

subject: sample_to_sample_noise
magnitude: Same field, five assay dates, same method (ASTM D8420/IP 389A): WAT 18.4 to 21.9 C, mean 20.2 C, SD 1.7 C
conditions: KG-D6 stabilised condensate, Bureau Veritas Dubai and others, 2023 to 2025
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv (Reliance tender assays)
notes: Combines lab repeatability, reproducibility and real sample drift. Use about 1.7 C SD as a lower bound on per-sample noise.

subject: pour_point
magnitude: WAT minus pour point = mean +26.8 C, median +23.6 C, SD 17.1 C, 10th to 90th percentile +5.0 to +55.0 C, range -11.5 to +72.2 C; WAT below pour point in 1.6% of rows
conditions: master_v9 rows with WAT and pour point, high-pressure tier X excluded, n=245, all methods
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: Linear fit WAT = 0.566*pour + 29.0 C, r = 0.70. Generator should enforce WAT > pour point almost always.

subject: pour_point
magnitude: Median WAT minus pour point by WAT method: DSC +17.5 C (n=39), D8420 +12.6 C (n=8), D2500 cloud point +13.0 C (n=13), pour tester torque +22.2 C (n=59, SD 5.2), uDSC +25.9 C (n=11), CPM +32.8 C (n=34), viscometry +44.4 C (n=35)
conditions: master_v9, non-X tiers; groups differ in oil types as well as method
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
where: wat_c minus pour_c by wat_method family
notes: Confounded by which oils each method was used on (viscometry and CPM sets include many very waxy oils), but the ordering DSC < CPM is consistent with the method offset.

subject: wax_content
conditions: master_v9, all methods, non-X tiers, wax by mixed methods (UOP46, acetone precipitation, GC, DSC)
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: Pooled across methods; scatter is large. Logarithmic shape is physically expected (ideal solubility).

subject: API
conditions: master_v9 non-X rows with API and WAT
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: API alone carries almost no information on WAT.

subject: crude_class
conditions: master_v9 non-X rows
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: Wax content separates WAT far better than API class.

subject: method_DSC_vs_viscometry
magnitude: DSC minus capillary viscometer = -2.25 and -1.95 C; polarising microscope minus viscometer = +7.6 and +8.5 C
conditions: Two Dabei (Tarim) condensates, wax 4.5 wt%, atmospheric pressure, Cao et al. 2022 Energies 15:6200 Tables 2 to 4
citation: Cao et al. (2022). Energies 15(17):6200, via master_v9.csv
notes: Ordering in this paper: microscope > viscometer > DSC.

subject: method_spread_same_oil
magnitude: Five methods on one oil span 45.95 to 50.33 C (4.4 C): DSC 45.95, NIR wavelength scan 47.71, refractive index 47.9, NIR temperature scan 48.63, polarised microscopy 50.33 C
conditions: Daqing-type DJ crude, wax 21.4 wt%, pour 33 C, CIESC Journal 2020 71(7):3333
citation: CIESC Journal (2020) 71(7):3333, via master_v9.csv
notes: NIR and refractive index sit between DSC and microscopy, about 2 C above DSC and 2 C below microscopy.

subject: inter_laboratory
magnitude: Same oil, three labs: ChevronTexaco 40.6 C, Total DSC 37.2 C, Tulsa DSC 35.0 C; DSC lab to lab difference 2.2 C, total spread 5.6 C
conditions: Cote Blanche crude (wax 6.3 wt%), DOE/Univ Tulsa report BC15150
citation: University of Tulsa DOE final report BC15150 (Paraffin deposition), via master_v9.csv

subject: cooling_rate
magnitude: DSC at 0.2 C/min gave 50.36 C vs 47.0 C at 2 C/min: -3.4 C for a tenfold faster cooling (different labs)
unit: C per decade of cooling rate
conditions: Caratinga crude (Brazil), Petrobras DSC 0.2 C/min vs Tulsa DSC 2 C/min
citation: University of Tulsa DOE final report BC15150, via master_v9.csv
notes: Lab effect and rate effect mixed; equals about -1.9 C per (C/min) if linear over 0.2 to 2 C/min.

subject: dissolved_gas_pressure
magnitude: Live oil at 2364 psia WAT 36.7 C vs stock tank oil at 15 psia 40.7 C: -4.0 C (about -0.25 C per MPa of live-oil pressure)
conditions: Nigerian crude LE-01, light transmission (laser solids detection), isobaric cooling, bubble point 1949 psia at 78 C; Uba, Ikeji and Onyekonwu 2004 SPE 88963
citation: Uba, Ikeji and Onyekonwu (2004). SPE 88963, Nigeria Annual International Conference, via master_v9.csv
notes: Pressure step 16.2 MPa; dissolved gas lowers WAT.

subject: method_ultrasonic
magnitude: Acoustic resonance first-crystal temperatures on degassed Uzen oils 64 to 84 C (median 72 C) vs light transmission 38 to 41.7 C at 12 MPa and DSC 48.4 C on Uzen oil from other studies
conditions: Uzen field Kazakhstan, Chandler 3000 GL PVT cell acoustic module, stepwise cooling 90 to 20 C; different wells and studies
citation: Nurlybai et al. (2026), via master_v9.csv; Energies 2026 19(5):1309; Sigitov et al. 2014
notes: Cross-study, different wells, so not a clean method offset; the acoustic values are about 20 to 30 C above other methods and may reflect the paraffin melting range rather than first appearance.

subject: detection_limit_viscometry
magnitude: Viscometry needs about 1 wt% crystals for a 2.5% deviation from Newtonian viscosity; critical crystal volume fraction estimated 0.3 to 0.5%
conditions: Analysis based on crystal axis ratios 15 to 20; authors say 1% solid is often enough to give a pour point, not a cloud point
citation: Coutinho, J.A.P. and Daridon, J.L. (2005). The limitations of the cloud point measurement techniques and the influence of the oil composition on its detection. Petroleum Science and Technology, 23, 1113-1128.
notes: So viscometric WAT should sit at the temperature where precipitated wax reaches roughly 0.3 to 1 wt%.

subject: detection_limit_CPM
magnitude: CPM detects a crystal of 0.5 to 1 micrometre depending on magnification; first nuclei by TEM are about 50 nm, far below CPM limit; filter plugging uses 0.5 micrometre filters
conditions: Review statement
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005). Pet Sci Technol 23:1113-1128.
notes: Filter plugging and light transmission need a significant quantity of crystals, so read lower than CPM.

subject: method_spread
magnitude: Cloud point error can be as much as 20 K depending on how much solid the method needs to detect
conditions: Review across techniques; larger for oils with long, slowly decaying n-paraffin tails
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005). Pet Sci Technol 23:1113-1128.

subject: method_light_transmission_vs_CPM
magnitude: CPM minus light transmission about 10 K (Table 2 entry 10.4 K, SD 0.6, ref Hammami and Raines 1997 SPE 38776); a second entry 6.1 K (SD 4.7, Ronningsen 1997)
conditions: Table 2 of Coutinho and Daridon 2005 compiling literature pairs; light transmittance at atmospheric pressure
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005), citing Hammami, A. and Raines, M. (1997) SPE 38776 and Ronningsen, Somme and Pedersen (1997) Multiphase 97
notes: Text states differences of the order of 10 K between light transmission and CPM. The 6.1 K cell placement inferred from a garbled table extraction.

subject: method_CPM_vs_DSC
magnitude: Literature mean CPM minus DSC differences (reconstructed Table 2): Ronningsen 1991 about 9.0 K (SD 6.9), Erickson 1993 about 14.6 K (SD 9.7), Monger-McClure 1999 about 1.3 K (SD 3.1), Cazaux 1998 about 6.0 K (SD 7.8), Kok 1996 about -1.2 K (SD 5.2)
conditions: Pairwise average differences between techniques from several studies, each over several oils
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005), Table 2, compiling Ronningsen et al. 1991, Erickson et al. 1993 SPE 26604, Monger-McClure et al. 1999, Cazaux et al. 1998 SPE 49213, Kok et al. 1996
where: Table 2 (layout garbled in text extraction; cell placement reconstructed)
notes: Placement of these values in the CPM-DSC cell is a reconstruction from the order of the extracted numbers; verify against the printed table. The same column also holds CPM vs viscosity values of 6.0 (Ronningsen), 13.2 (Erickson), 5.4 (Cazaux), 0.7 (Kok) K.

subject: method_CPM_vs_viscometry
magnitude: Literature mean CPM minus viscometry (reconstructed Table 2): Ronningsen 1991 about 6.0 K (SD 4.7), Erickson 1993 about 13.2 K (SD 8.4), Cazaux 1998 about 5.4 K (SD 6.9), Kok 1996 about 0.7 K (SD 3.9)
conditions: Pairwise averages over several oils per study
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005), Table 2
notes: Our own ANS data give median CPM minus viscometry +1.1 C, near the Kok value.

subject: cooling_rate
magnitude: Empirical correction equal to the cooling rate in K/min has been applied to DSC WAT (Monger-McClure 1999), i.e. about +1 K per (K/min); 0.1 to 0.5 K/min gives negligible deviation from equilibrium in small cells; 5 to 10 K/min gives considerable supercooling
conditions: DSC; Ronningsen 1991 suggests the effect may be much larger
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005), citing Monger-McClure, Tackett and Merrill (1999) SPE Prod Facil 14(1)
notes: Generator: measured DSC WAT = true WAT minus about 1 C times cooling rate in C/min, plus extra for fast rates.

subject: WDT
magnitude: WDT minus WAT about 15 K for DSC and about 10 K for microscopy
conditions: Review statement, typical crude oils
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005). Pet Sci Technol 23:1113-1128.
notes: Our master gives median 8.2 C (all), 8.0 C CPM, 12.1 C DSC (Kok 2018); consistent ordering.

subject: sample_handling
magnitude: Cooling a model oil to 320 K during sampling removes all n-paraffins above C50, about 1% of total wax, which changes the measured cloud point
conditions: Simulated Oil A (15% wax, decay 0.92, up to C90) becoming Oil E (13.77% wax, up to C50)
citation: Coutinho and Daridon (2005). Pet Sci Technol 23:1113-1128.
notes: The heaviest tail controls WAT; losing it lowers WAT while barely changing wax content.

subject: detection_limit_general
magnitude: Estimated detection limits of cloud point techniques 0.01 to 0.1 mass % solid out of solution depending on technique; CPM resolves crystals of about 1 micrometre
conditions: Review
citation: Hammami, A., Ratulowski, J. and Coutinho, J.A.P. (2003). Cloud points: can we measure or model them? Petroleum Science and Technology, 21(3-4), 345-358.
notes: CPM is more sensitive than DSC and light transmittance, so those give cloud points further inside the solid-liquid envelope.

subject: precipitation_rate
magnitude: Most techniques agree within +/-3 C for oils precipitating wax fast (about 0.4 mass% per C); Gulf of Mexico oils precipitating about ten times slower show strong method dependence
conditions: Kruka, Cadena and Long 1995 JPT 47:681, cited
citation: Hammami, Ratulowski and Coutinho (2003), citing Kruka et al. (1995) JPT 47:681
notes: Key generator rule: method offset is roughly (detection threshold in wt%) divided by (precipitation slope in wt% per C). At 0.4 wt%/C and a 1 wt% threshold the offset is 2.5 C; at 0.04 wt%/C it becomes 25 C.

subject: WDT
magnitude: At scan rate 0.01 C/min the gap between crystallisation onset and dissolution end is about 3 to 4 C (Gimzewski and Audley 1993); WDT should be measured at heating below 1 C/min
conditions: Very slow scanning, cited result
citation: Hammami, Ratulowski and Coutinho (2003), citing Gimzewski and Audley (1993) Thermochim Acta
notes: Minimum hysteresis even near equilibrium.

subject: inter_laboratory
magnitude: DeepStar cloud point round robin: differences of at least 10 F (5.6 C) between labs and techniques on the same samples
conditions: Three samples sent to several labs, DeepStar II report DSII CTR 902-1 (1995)
citation: Hunt, A. (1996). Uncertainties remain in predicting paraffin deposition. Oil and Gas Journal, 29 July 1996.

subject: cooling_rate
magnitude: DSC WAT 16.53 C at 0.2 C/min vs 13.87 C at 1.0 C/min: -2.66 C, i.e. -3.3 C per (C/min)
conditions: Pennsylvania crude A, TA Instruments DSC, sample 10.5 +/- 0.5 mg
citation: TA Instruments. TA429: Determination of wax appearance temperature (WAT) for crude oil and petroleum products using DSC. Application note.

subject: cooling_rate
magnitude: DSC first-transition onset -11.19, -13.57, -14.51, -16.19, -17.33 C at 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10 C/min: linear slope -0.64 C per (C/min), or -2.54 C per ln unit of rate
conditions: Alaska crude C, TA DSC, 10.5 mg; second transition barely moves (slope -0.04)
citation: TA Instruments. TA429 application note.
notes: Fit done here on the five Table 1 points. Rate effect is larger per unit at slow rates, so a log law fits better than a linear one.

subject: method_spread_same_oil
magnitude: Rheometry minus DSC +12.9 and +9.9 C (RDO1, RDO2) but -11.7 C (J32); FTIR minus DSC -0.4, -2.0, +2.7 C; densitometry minus DSC +7.8, +2.5 C (not detectable for J32)
conditions: Three Mexican crudes; DSC 19.2, 18.5, 28 C; rheometry 32.1, 28.4, 16.3 C; densitometry 27, 21, ND; FTIR 18.8, 16.5, 30.7 C; DSC scans at 5 C/min
citation: Alcazar-Vara, L.A. and Buenrostro-Gonzalez, E. (2013). Liquid-solid phase equilibria of paraffinic systems by DSC measurements. In: Applications of Calorimetry in a Wide Context, InTech, ch. 11, Table 5 (data from their 2011 Fuel Process Technol paper).
notes: FTIR again tracks DSC within about 2 to 3 C, matching Bouzas 2011.

subject: precision_D8420
magnitude: ASTM D8420 interim repeatability: WAT 1.96 C, WDT 2.39 C; reproducibility not yet determined; no bias
conditions: 2 labs, 20 samples (ULSD and VLSFO, viscosity 5.7 to 384.5 mm2/s, pour 9 to 33 C, WAT 34 to 60 C), 5 repeats; cooling and warming 1.5 +/- 0.5 C/min; NIR light scattering detection; range -30 to +75 C
citation: ASTM D8420-21. Standard test method for determination of wax appearance temperature and wax disappearance temperature by optical light scattering detection (sample pages).
notes: Repeatability r 1.96 C means the standard deviation of a single result is about 1.96/2.77 = 0.71 C.

subject: precision_D3117
magnitude: ASTM D3117 wax appearance point (visual, stirred): repeatability 0.8 C, reproducibility 2.2 C; cooling 1 to 2 C/min, preferred 1.5 C/min
conditions: Distillate fuels (burner, diesel, turbine); 8 fuels in precision study, also tested by D2500
citation: ASTM D3117-03. Standard test method for wax appearance point of distillate fuels (sample pages).
notes: Fuels, not crude oils; lower bound on noise.

subject: method_D2500
magnitude: D2500 applies only to samples transparent in 40 mm layers with cloud point below 49 C; read at each 1 C step; precision stated for D1500 colour 3.5 or lower
conditions: Cloud point of petroleum products; stepwise baths 0, -18, -33 C
citation: ASTM D2500-23. Standard test method for cloud point of petroleum products and liquid fuels (sample pages).
notes: On dark crude oils D2500 is outside its scope; results quantised to 1 C.

subject: precision_D2500
magnitude: D2500 cloud point repeatability 2 C, reproducibility 4 C (distillates)
conditions: Distillate fuels within scope
citation: ASTM D2500 precision section (not read; recalled)
notes: Precision section was not in the sample pages; verify.

subject: precision_light_scattering
magnitude: Phase Technology optical WAT analyser repeatable within 1.0 C; Arabian Medium crude WAT 25.1 C, WDT 43.9 C (WDT minus WAT 18.8 C); thin layer under 1 mm; 20 to 40 min per test
conditions: Vendor white paper, crude oils including opaque
citation: Phase Technology (PAC). White paper: Wax appearance temperature of crude oils.
notes: Vendor claim; says DSC WAT tends to be lower.

subject: cooling_rate
magnitude: Rheometric WAT = -0.739*ln(cooling rate in C/s) + 31.141 C (R2 0.9935) for 30 wt% wax in kerosene: about 36.2 C at 0.001 C/s and 34.8 C at 0.007 C/s
conditions: Model wax-kerosene solution, plate rheometer, gap 0.4 mm
citation: Struchkov, I.A. and Rogachev, M.K. (2017). Wax precipitation in multicomponent hydrocarbon system. J Pet Explor Prod Technol 7:543-553.
notes: Model system, not crude oil. Also gap effect WAT = -1.214 ln(gap mm) + 31.579 and shear effect +0.26 C per ln(1/s).

subject: mechanical_impurities
magnitude: Adding 0.25 to 2 g/L solids raised rheometric WAT from 33.1 C to 34.1 to 36.5 C (+1.0 to +3.4 C; calcite largest, kaolinite smallest)
conditions: 30 wt% wax in kerosene, rheometer
citation: Struchkov and Rogachev (2017). J Pet Explor Prod Technol 7:543-553.
notes: Field samples with sand or fines may read high.

subject: water_cut
magnitude: WAT rose from 24.1 C at 0% water to 34.1 C at 90% water cut (about +0.11 C per % water)
conditions: 10 wt% wax in kerosene emulsions, rheometer
citation: Struchkov and Rogachev (2017). J Pet Explor Prod Technol 7:543-553.
notes: Rheometric WAT in emulsions is affected by the viscosity rise, so this may be partly a method artefact.

subject: pressure_dead
magnitude: Visual (HP microscope) WAT in gas-free model solutions rises with pressure as about exp(P/175.75), P in MPa: roughly +0.57% of WAT per MPa (about +0.2 C/MPa at WAT 35 C)
conditions: Wax 10 to 60 wt% in kerosene, 0.1 to 40 MPa, no dissolved gas
citation: Struchkov and Rogachev (2017). J Pet Explor Prod Technol 7:543-553.
notes: Equation rendering was garbled in the extraction; the per-MPa value is derived here.

subject: method_spread
magnitude: Under preferred operating conditions, cloud points by each of four methods agreed with the all-method average within 3 F (1.7 C); duplicate samples by the same method reproduced within about 5 F (2.8 C)
conditions: DeepStar Gulf of Mexico oils, four laboratory cloud point methods, slow cooling
citation: Monger-McClure, T.G., Tackett, J.E. and Merrill, L.S. (1997). DeepStar comparisons of cloud point measurement and paraffin prediction methods. SPE 38774, SPE ATCE (journal version SPE Prod Facil 14(1), 1999).
notes: Agreement is good only when cooling is slow or corrected; methods are not named in the abstract (from Coutinho 2005 Table 2 they include CPM, DSC, FTIR, filter plugging, D2500).

subject: cooling_rate
magnitude: Supercooling correction of about 2 times the cooling rate in F/min was added when very slow cooling was not possible; equals about +2 C per (C/min)
conditions: DeepStar lab cloud points (DSC and others)
citation: Monger-McClure, Tackett and Merrill (1997). SPE 38774.
notes: 2 F per (F/min) = 2*1.8 F per (C/min) = 3.6 F = 2.0 C per (C/min). Coutinho and Daridon 2005 report the correction as equal to the rate in K/min; the abstract wording supports the larger factor.

subject: pressure_dead
magnitude: Dead (stabilised) condensate WAT 27 C at 1 bar to 38 C at 352 bar: linear slope +0.28 C per MPa; WDT slope +0.24 C per MPa (37 to 46 C)
conditions: Quartz crystal microbalance, 1 C steps with 0.5 h hold, +/-1 C; one North Sea type condensate
citation: Burgass, R.W. (2015). Applications of quartz crystal microbalance technology in petroleum engineering. PhD thesis, Heriot-Watt University, Tables 2.6 and 2.7.
notes: Slopes fitted here on the tabulated points.

subject: dissolved_gas_pressure
magnitude: Live condensate WAT 29 to 33 C vs dead 32.6 to 36.8 C at the same pressure (96 to 301 bar): live minus dead about -3.6 to -3.9 C; above bubble point (101 bar) live WAT rises at +0.19 C per MPa
conditions: QCM, same condensate recombined with gas, bubble point 101 bar at 15 C
citation: Burgass (2015). PhD thesis, Heriot-Watt University, Tables 2.6, 2.7.
notes: Dead values interpolated to the live pressures here. Below the bubble point live WAT stays flat near 29 C between 58 and 96 bar.

subject: WDT
magnitude: WDT minus WAT about 8 C average for both dead and live condensate by QCM; 10 C at 1 bar (27 vs 37 C)
conditions: QCM step cooling and heating
citation: Burgass (2015). PhD thesis, Heriot-Watt University.

subject: cooling_rate
magnitude: In Ronningsen 1991 (17 North Sea oils) microscopy at 0.5 C/min gave the highest WAT; DSC run at 10 C/min was often below viscometric WAT, by more than 20 C for some oils
conditions: Cited summary
citation: Burgass (2015), citing Ronningsen et al. (1991) Energy Fuels 5:895
notes: Fast DSC (10 C/min) strongly underestimates.

subject: pressure_dead
magnitude: Pure n-C14, n-C15, n-C16 melting/WDT rise about +0.21 to +0.22 C per MPa from 0.1 to 100 MPa (nearly linear)
conditions: Correlation outputs fitted to Milhet et al. high-pressure data
citation: Moradi, G., Mohadesi, M. and Mokhtari, M. (2013). A new correlation for prediction of wax disappearance temperature of hydrocarbon mixtures at various pressures. J Chem Pet Eng (Univ Tehran) 47(1):27-38.
notes: Gas-free systems: about +2 C per 10 MPa is the baseline compressional effect.

subject: WDT
magnitude: Optical WAT-WDT analyser on 35 opaque crude and diesel samples; Heavy Louisiana Sweet and Lula have similar WAT but HLS WDT is more than 13 C warmer; Peace River No.1 and No.2 WATs differ by more than 18 C
conditions: Light scattering method (basis ASTM D5773 / later D8420), precision 1.0 C
citation: Oil and Gas Journal. Modified test method measures wax deposition qualities of opaque crude.
notes: WDT minus WAT is oil-specific and not a constant.

subject: pressure_dead
magnitude: Degassed condensate WAT rises linearly with pressure: +0.186 C/MPa (well A, 32.4 to 45.7 C over 0.1 to 70 MPa) and +0.178 C/MPa (well B, 34.1 to 46.6 C)
conditions: Dabei condensates (wax 9.0 and 6.8 wt% by crystallisation), high-pressure polarising microscope, heated to 55 C first
citation: Cao et al. (2022). Energies 15(17):6200, Table 7.
notes: Slopes fitted here on all 8 points (R2 near 1). Agrees with Burgass QCM (+0.28) and pure n-alkanes (+0.22).

subject: dissolved_gas_pressure
magnitude: Gas-saturated (equilibrium) condensate WAT falls -0.193 and -0.198 C/MPa as saturation pressure rises to 35 to 40 MPa (GOR 0 to 264 and 0 to 322 Sm3/m3); live minus dead at same pressure = -1.6 C at 5 MPa, -3.7 C at 10 MPa, -7.5 to -7.9 C at 20 MPa, -11.1 C at 30 MPa, -12.7 to -15.1 C at 35 to 40 MPa; about -0.047 C per Sm3/m3 of GOR relative to dead oil at same pressure, or -0.025 C per Sm3/m3 relative to atmospheric dead WAT
conditions: Dabei A and B condensates, constant mass expansion, polarising microscope
citation: Cao et al. (2022). Energies 15(17):6200, Table 7.
notes: Derived here by interpolating degassed WAT at each pressure. Dissolved gas dominates compression for gas-rich fluids.

subject: precipitation_rate
magnitude: Maximum wax precipitation rate only 0.16 to 0.18 % per C drop, reached at 7.6 to 8.7 C; DSC wax 3.96 to 4.48 wt%; the low rate explains a microscope minus DSC gap of about 10 C
conditions: Dabei condensates, DSC with 200 J/g average crystallisation heat
citation: Cao et al. (2022). Energies 15(17):6200, Tables 3, 4.
notes: Supports the rule offset = detection threshold / precipitation slope.

subject: method_flow_loop_vs_light_transmission
magnitude: Dynamic flow-loop deposition onset 2 to 4 C higher than optical (light transmittance) WAT; flow loop initial onset 41.0 to 44.0 C vs optical 38.0 to 41.7 C; bulk onset in loop 33.5 to 35.0 C
conditions: Uzen 13th horizon oil, four wells; optical at 12 MPa with stirring; loop 2 mm ID at 0.5 m/s, 0.2 C per hour steps
citation: Comparative analysis of methods for wax crystallization onset in Uzen oil. Energies (2026) 19(5):1309.
notes: Cold-wall methods (flow loop, cold finger) can read above bulk WAT because of wall gradients.

subject: method_DSC_vs_FTIR
magnitude: Thesis table: DSC minus FTIR = +1, 0, +0.5, +1, +11.0 (CP5 double-peak), -0.5, +0.5, -0.5, +0.5, +1.0 C; mean +0.39 C, SD 0.6 C excluding CP5; CP5 FTIR repeat 27.7 +/- 0.6 C
conditions: 10 Spanish refinery crudes (5 paraffinic, 5 naphthenic), FTIR on heating at 5 C/min
citation: Bouzas Gonzalez (2011). WAT of crude oils by FTIR. Thesis, Universidad Rey Juan Carlos.
notes: FTIR values here differ from master_v9 rows R299 to R317 for CP2 (38 vs 42), CP3 (30.5 vs 30), CN1 (31.5 vs 32), CN4 (29 vs 28), CN5 (30 vs 31) and CP5 (28 vs 34); master may come from a different table or rounding; flag for checking.

subject: wax_content
magnitude: WAT = 2.10*(DSC precipitable n-paraffin, %) + 16.9 C (r = 0.60, n=10); n-paraffin 2.7 to 8.5 % vs WAT 18.5 to 39 C
conditions: 10 Spanish refinery crudes, DSC WAT and DSC solid wax
citation: Bouzas Gonzalez (2011), URJC thesis; regression fitted here
notes: Equal wax gives different WAT depending on chain length (CP4 26 C vs CP5 39 C at 7.2%).

subject: method_CPM_vs_viscometry
magnitude: ANS crude: viscometric WPT 6 C below CPM WPT; DSC at 10 C/min could not identify any WPT; CPM duplicates SD 0.4 C (1 micron detection, 15 min holds, 1 C steps)
conditions: Alaska North Slope crude, capillary viscometer 100 to 1000 1/s, centrifuge solids 0.2 wt% at 21 C, 2.6 wt% at -1 C, 6.2 wt% at -18 C
citation: US Patent 6841779 B1. Measurement of wax precipitation temperature and precipitated solid weight percent versus temperature by infrared spectroscopy.
notes: Slow-precipitating ANS oil: only 0.2 wt% solid at 21 C, so DSC misses the onset.

subject: precision_FTIR
magnitude: FTIR WPT on model oil: mean 20 C, SD 0.76 C over six aliquots vs reference 20.35 C; wt% solid RSD within 10%
conditions: n-C10 plus C20 to C30 model oil, 0.05 to 0.20 C/min
citation: US Patent 6841779 B1.

subject: gel_point
magnitude: Gulf of Mexico crude gelled near room temperature at about 2 wt% precipitated solids (FTIR estimate 1 to 2 wt%)
conditions: GoM crude, FTIR solid estimate
citation: US Patent 6841779 B1.
notes: Pour/gel point sits where solid wax reaches about 2 wt%; WAT is where solid starts. Gap WAT minus pour equals about 2 wt% divided by precipitation slope.

subject: WAT_multiple_events
magnitude: uDSC first WAT minus second WAT = 13.7 to 21.9 C (AP01 19.5, AP02 13.7, AP04 12.0, AP07 14.0, AP08 21.9, AP09 21.9 C); oils with no n-alkanes C15 to C44 (AP05, AP06) still show WAT about 20 C
conditions: Nine Brazilian crudes, uDSC cooling 0.48 C/min from 80 to -10 C
citation: Oliveira et al. (2018). Wax behavior in crude oils by pour point analyses. J Braz Chem Soc.
notes: If a method picks up the second, larger event (e.g. a less sensitive one), it reports a WAT 12 to 22 C lower. Pour point minus first WAT here ranges -16.5 to -45.6 C.

subject: method_NIR_vs_CPM
magnitude: NIR scattering at 1100 nm can detect crystallites smaller than 55 nm vs about 0.5 micrometre for CPM; NIR WAT values similar to CPM
conditions: Waxy crude oil, waxy gas condensate, paraffin in dodecane model fluids; works under flowing and equilibrium conditions; needs correction for crude oil attenuation in opaque oils
citation: Paso, K.G., Kallevik, H. and Sjoblom, J. (2009). Measurement of wax appearance temperature using near-infrared (NIR) scattering. Energy and Fuels, 23(10), 4988-4994.
notes: Our DJ crude pair gives NIR minus CPM = -1.7 and -2.6 C, so NIR is about 2 C below CPM there.

subject: detection_limit_light_transmission
magnitude: Laser solids detection (SDS) WAT corresponds to calculated solid wax of 0.16 wt% (oil A-1), 0.19 wt% (A-10) and 0.43 wt% (A-2); calculated WAT about 3 C below CPM/field WAT for A-1 and 1.7 C above CPM for A-10
conditions: Hammami and Raines GoM fluids compared with a thermodynamic model
citation: Coutinho, J.A.P., Edmonds, B., Moorwood, T., Szczepanski, R. and Zhang, X. (2006). Reliable wax predictions for flow assurance. Energy and Fuels, 20, 1081-1088.
notes: Model-inferred thresholds; light transmission needs roughly 0.2 to 0.4 wt% solid.

subject: detection_limit_filter_plugging
magnitude: Live-oil WAT from 1 micrometre filter pressure-drop discontinuity matched the calculated 1 wt% solid wax line
conditions: Ronningsen oil 10, live, filter method
citation: Coutinho et al. (2006). Energy and Fuels, 20, 1081-1088.
notes: Filter plugging WAT sits where about 1 wt% wax has formed.

subject: method_spread
magnitude: Erickson oil 6: measured WAT 23 C while model predicts only 0.025 wt% wax at 23 C and a thermodynamic WAT about 11 C higher
conditions: Slow-precipitating oil
citation: Coutinho et al. (2006). Energy and Fuels, 20, 1081-1088.
notes: Thermodynamic WAT can exceed measured WAT by about 10 C for oils with long, dilute paraffin tails.

subject: precision_general
magnitude: Good modern WAT measurements carry about +/-5 F (+/-2.8 C) uncertainty; older measurements considerably more; Daridon oils about 2 K
conditions: Review statement citing Monger-McClure et al.
citation: Coutinho et al. (2006), citing Monger-McClure et al. (1999)
notes: Use about 1.5 to 2 C SD as total measurement noise.

subject: n_paraffin_tail
magnitude: Cutting the upper n-paraffin limit by one or two carbon numbers brought predicted WAT down to the measured values for Daridon oil A
conditions: Thermodynamic model vs measured WAT
citation: Coutinho et al. (2006). Energy and Fuels, 20, 1081-1088.
notes: WAT is controlled by the heaviest few n-paraffins.

subject: method_rheology_vs_microCT
magnitude: WAT by rheology (open system, 1 C/min, 5 1/s) and by micro-CT in core differed by 3 to 4 C
conditions: One waxy crude, 4.1 MPa confining pressure in core test
citation: Formation damage induced by wax deposition: laboratory investigations and modeling (2020). J Pet Explor Prod Technol.

subject: detection_limit_DSC
magnitude: Conventional DSC registers WAT only after roughly 0.1 to 0.5 wt% wax has crystallised (heat of about 200 J/g gives a weak signal); micro-DSC is more sensitive
conditions: General statement; sensitivity scales with cooling rate and sample mass
citation: Commonly stated in WAT method reviews (e.g. Hammami, Ratulowski and Coutinho 2003; Coutinho and Daridon 2005), exact figure not read
notes: Consistent with Hammami 2003 overall range 0.01 to 0.1 wt% being for the most sensitive methods, and with DSC sitting below CPM by 2 to 10 C in our own same-oil pairs. Verify.

subject: wax_content
magnitude: WAT minus pour point = -0.50*wax + 26.5 C (r = -0.41, n=163); median gap 23.4 C for wax under 5 wt% (n=75), 21.4 C for 5 to 20 wt% (n=56), 12.2 C for wax 20 wt% or more (n=32)
conditions: master_v9 non-X rows with WAT, pour and wax
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: Pour point rises faster with wax (+1.61 C per wt%, r=0.71) than WAT does, so high-wax oils have a narrow WAT-pour gap. Generator should use a wax-dependent gap.

subject: wax_content
magnitude: WAT vs wax slope by WAT method: DSC 0.68 C/wt% (n=59, r=0.50, log form 8.1 ln(wax)+15.4); CPM 1.40 C/wt% (n=18, r=0.78, 12.4 ln(wax)+16.7); uDSC 2.63 C/wt% (n=10, r=0.91, 19.6 ln(wax)+10.5)
conditions: master_v9 non-X rows
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: Different oil sets per method; viscometry rows show no wax trend (n=13).

subject: viscosity_40C
magnitude: WAT = 5.96*ln(kinematic viscosity at 40 C, cSt) + 23.1 C (r = 0.61, n=67)
conditions: master_v9 non-X rows with viscosity
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: Waxy oils near or below WAT at 40 C show inflated viscosity, so this link partly reflects wax itself.

subject: pour_point
magnitude: Malaysian crude: WAT 32 C, pour point 3 C (gap 29 C), wax 20.58 wt%, asphaltenes 12.13%, density 0.8509 g/cm3, 5.15 mPa.s at 40 C
conditions: One crude, cold finger study
citation: Kamisan, M.G. and Hussin, H. (n.d.). The effect of aging on critical carbon number during wax deposition analysis. UiTM.
notes: Possible new data row for the harvest team (WAT method not stated).

subject: asphaltenes
magnitude: 0.1 to 1 g/L asphaltenes lowered DSC WAT from 27.9 C to 26.1 to 27.2 C: -0.7 to -1.8 C (SD 0.1 to 0.5 C); interfacially active and remaining asphaltenes behave alike
conditions: Model oil 100 g/L n-C28 in 6:4 dodecane:toluene, DSC 5 C/min after 1 h at 60 C
citation: Ali, A., Yaghy, G., Parameswaran, L., Hodges, C.S., Charpentier, T.V.J., Connell, S.D., Roberts, K.J. and Harbottle, D. (2024). The contrasting behavior of strongly and weakly interfacially active asphaltenes on the rheology of model waxy oils. Energy and Fuels, 38, 117-126.
notes: Asphaltene effect on WAT is small (1 to 2 C) and saturates at low concentration.

subject: asphaltenes
magnitude: 0.05 wt% asphaltenes lowered DSC WAT from 25 to 24 C (-1 C); 0.15 to 1.5 wt% did not lower it further; gel point 22 C lowered by 0.6 to 1.2 C
conditions: 10 wt% wax in xylene, DSC 10 C/min; gel point by rheology 0.5 C/min
citation: Li, Y., Li, C., Zhao, Z., Cai, W., Xia, X., Yao, B., Sun, G. and Yang, F. (2022). Effects of asphaltene concentration and test temperature on the stability of water-in-model waxy crude oil emulsions. ACS Omega, 7, 8023-8035.
notes: Generator: asphaltene term on WAT at most about -1 to -2 C, not proportional to asphaltene content.

subject: asphaltenes
magnitude: Cited: Kriz and Andersen found WAT rose at 0.01 wt% asphaltenes and fell significantly at 0.02 wt%; Oliveira and Lucas found asphaltenes act like a pour point depressant with almost no effect on WAT
conditions: Literature review in a deposition paper; base crude WAT 40 C by DSC at 5 C/min, wax 15.36 wt%, resins 3.2, aromatics 20.1 wt%
citation: Lei, Y. et al. (2023). Effect of existence state of asphaltenes on the asphaltenes-wax interaction in wax deposition. Petroleum Science, 20, 507-514.
notes: Direction of asphaltene effect depends on dispersion state; magnitude small.

subject: dissolved_gas_type
magnitude: Under high gas pressure CO2 and natural gas reduce WAT while nitrogen has virtually no effect; ATR FT-IR WAT lower than viscometry, MRI and CPM values on the same crude
conditions: One waxy crude, ATR FT-IR CH2 rocking band ratio method, ambient and high pressure
citation: Shalygin, A.S., Kozhevnikov, I.V., Morozov, E.V. and Martyanov, O.N. (2024). Features of wax appearance temperature determination of waxy crude oil using ATR FT-IR spectroscopy under ambient and high pressure. Applied Spectroscopy, 78(3), 277-288.
notes: Numbers only in full text (not open). N2 pressure acts like plain compression (small positive shift).

subject: dissolved_gas_pressure
magnitude: Ultrasonic method: live oil WAT 8 C lower than dead oil WAT at the same pressure; live oil WAT at reservoir pressure about 3.7 C lower than stock tank oil WAT by a conventional method; lowering pressure reduces WAT of both live and dead oil (above bubble point)
conditions: High pour point waxy oil (China), ultrasonic head-wave frequency turning point, reservoir conditions
citation: Measurement of the wax appearance temperature of waxy oil under the reservoir condition with ultrasonic method (2014). Petroleum Exploration and Development, August 2014.
notes: Possibly the Jiang et al. 2014 source named in the brief; authors not shown on DOAJ page. Pressure raising WAT plus gas lowering WAT partly cancel at reservoir pressure (net -3.7 C).

subject: dissolved_gas_type
magnitude: At 21 MPa, Petrukhnovskoe crude (32 wt% wax) WAT 63 C; adding 10 wt% CO2 gave 62 C (-1 C); adding 10 wt% N2 about 2 C lower
conditions: High-pressure microscopy / light scattering, reservoir pressure 21 MPa
citation: Struchkov, I.A., Rogachev, M.K., Kalinin, E.S. and Roschin, P.V. (2019). Investigations of temperature and dilution effect on rheological properties of waxy crude oil. J Pet Explor Prod Technol 9.
notes: Author list beyond Struchkov not verified. Small gas additions by mass shift WAT by only 1 to 2 C in a very waxy oil. Rheometric WAT at 1 atm could not be fixed precisely (lattice near 50 C).

subject: solvent_aromatic_light_fraction
magnitude: Same wax in diesel gives WAT 2 to 4 C higher than in kerosene; rheological WAT about 1 C above visual WAT; 0.1 to 1 g/L kaolinite raises WAT about 1 to 2 C
conditions: Paraffin wax 10 to 60 wt% in kerosene or diesel, HP microscope and rotational viscometer, atmospheric
citation: Struchkov et al. (2019). J Pet Explor Prod Technol.
notes: A heavier, less solvating liquid matrix raises WAT; losing light ends works the same way.

subject: within_oil_pairs
magnitude: master_v9: 39 oil groups have WAT by 2 or more methods, giving 276 within-oil pairs (58 same-source). Same-source mean differences: CPM minus DSC +6.1 C (n=5), DSC minus FTIR +0.45 C (n=10), CPM minus viscometry +0.7 C (n=19 incl. history-kept), DSC minus viscometry -2.1 C (n=2), CPM minus NIR +2.2 C (n=2), DSC minus NIR -2.2 C (n=2), CPM minus refractive index +2.4 C, CPM minus densitometry +1.0 C
conditions: Pairs file agents/effects/within_oil_pairs.csv; same_source flag marks pairs from the same paper; pressure_involved flag marks high-pressure rows
citation: Own analysis of master_v9.csv
notes: Cross-source pairs (e.g. Uzen ultrasonic vs others, Penara CPM 63 to 68 C vs DSC 37 C) are dominated by sample and lab differences and should not be used as method offsets.
